summary: Defines the LDAPv3 schema for representing UDDI version 3 data in an LDAP directory. It specifies object classes, attributes, and containment rules to model UDDI entities. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: UDDI is a business directory for web services. This explains how to store that directory's entries in a different kind of directory.

questions: what is ldap schema for uddi
how to store uddi data in ldap
subtitle: Maps UDDI business directories into LDAP schema for unified storage

tldr.problem: UDDI registries describe web services and businesses, but organizations often store such data in LDAP directories instead. There was no standard way to represent UDDI concepts as LDAP entries.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines LDAP object classes, attributes, and containment rules that model UDDI entities like businessEntity, businessService, bindingTemplate, and tModel, allowing UDDI data to be stored and retrieved via LDAP.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now manage UDDI data within their existing LDAP infrastructure while maintaining compatibility with UDDI systems, supporting integrated business service discovery.

today: RFC 4403 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. LDAP and UDDI registries remain used in enterprise environments, though modern service discovery often uses newer approaches like service meshes and container orchestration platforms.

sections.title: UDDI in LDAP Directories
sections.content:
The RFC defines how to represent Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration version 3 (UDDI) data structures within an LDAP directory. UDDI is a Web services registry where businesses publish information about themselves and the services they offer. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a general-purpose directory service used by many organizations to store and retrieve information about users, computers, and other resources. This RFC bridges the two by specifying LDAP object classes and attributes that correspond to UDDI concepts.

The goal is to allow organizations that manage UDDI data to do so using their existing LDAP infrastructure rather than maintaining separate UDDI-specific systems, while preserving the ability to exchange data with UDDI systems using standard formats.
sections.plainLanguage: UDDI registries and LDAP directories are like two different filing cabinets with different drawer labels. This document explains how to relabel LDAP's drawers so you can use them for UDDI's files.

sections.title: Core UDDI Data Structures
sections.content:
The RFC maps five main UDDI structures into LDAP:

businessEntity is the top-level container representing a business or organization. It holds descriptive information and references to the services that entity offers.

businessService represents a logical business service within an entity. One business may offer multiple services, and each service can contain multiple technical binding descriptions.

bindingTemplate provides technical details about how to access a service, including access points (URLs), hosted service references, and categorization information. It also references tModel instances for compatibility and technical specification details.

tModel (technical model) is keyed metadata that serves as a reference system, typically used to define compatibility requirements or to point to specifications and documentation for a service.

publisherAssertion describes relationships between businessEntity objects, allowing related businesses to make their connections visible in the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of these like organization levels: a company (businessEntity) has departments (businessService), each department has contact methods (bindingTemplate), each contact method points to a handbook (tModel), and you can note which companies are related (publisherAssertion).

sections.title: Attribute and Object Class Design
sections.content:
The RFC defines approximately 46 LDAP attribute types to represent UDDI data elements. Key attributes include uddiBusinessKey, uddiServiceKey, uddiBindingKey, and uddiTModelKey, which serve as unique identifiers corresponding to their respective UDDI concepts. Other attributes carry descriptive information such as uddiName, uddiDescription, and uddiCategoryBag for categorization using standards like NAICS and UNSPC.

For UDDIv3 support, the RFC adds attributes with the uddiv3 prefix that accommodate version 3 features, including digital signatures, subscription information, and enhanced key management. Both v2 and v3 forms of keys are supported for backward compatibility.

The document defines 10 structural object classes corresponding to UDDI entities. Each object class specifies which attributes are mandatory (MUST) and which are optional (MAY), ensuring valid LDAP entries conform to UDDI data semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP needs labels for each type of information. The RFC defines what labels are needed (like "business name", "service description") and whether they're required or optional for each record type.

sections.title: Directory Hierarchy and Name Forms
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how UDDI structures are organized hierarchically within an LDAP directory tree. A uddiBusinessEntity can contain zero or more uddiContact and uddiBusinessService entries. Each uddiContact can contain uddiAddress entries. Each uddiBusinessService can contain uddiBindingTemplate entries, which in turn can contain uddiTModelInstanceInfo entries.

Name forms define the naming attribute for each object class. For example, a businessEntity is named by its uddiBusinessKey, ensuring unique identification within the directory. DIT (Directory Information Tree) structure rules enforce the allowed parent-child relationships, so for instance, a contact can only exist as a child of a business entity, and a binding template can only exist as a child of a business service.

This hierarchical structure preserves the parent-child relationships found in native UDDI data, allowing clients to navigate the directory and understand the containment relationships that UDDI defines.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like organizing files in folders: companies go at the top level, services go inside companies, technical details go inside services. The rules prevent putting a service in the wrong place.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that LDAP directory entries containing UDDI data become accessible via directory access mechanisms and subject to directory access control policies. When UDDI data is stored in LDAP, it may be examined and modified by directory access control mechanisms. Publishers can digitally sign UDDI entities using XML signatures before storing them in the directory, and clients can validate these signatures to ensure integrity.

Each UDDI entity has a uddiAuthorizedName attribute containing an LDAP DN that identifies the publisher or owner. The referenced LDAP object can provide the public key for validating signatures. Support for LDAP authentication and encryption mechanisms (TLS) is recommended to protect sensitive information like service access points.

The RFC also references IANA procedures for registering object identifiers (OIDs) for the schema elements, ensuring the schema definitions are officially recognized and avoiding conflicts with other LDAP schemas.
sections.plainLanguage: Since UDDI data in LDAP is like real company secrets, you need to control who can see it, verify it hasn't been tampered with, and protect it while it travels across networks.
